goals: Mechanistic: quantify the strength of soil-texture control on ELM sub-surface drainage (QDRAI) across the agricultural landscape
Validation: check simulated hydrologic state against available in-domain observations

model_choice.rationale: Soil-texture control on sub-surface drainage is a native ELM single-column sensitivity, resolvable by stratifying columns across dominant textures under a common forcing.

answerable: Strength of soil-texture control on sub-surface drainage flux (QDRAI) via stratified single-column runs under uniform forcing
Ranking of texture classes by drainage magnitude and seasonality

not_answerable.aspect: Direct validation of simulated sub-surface / tile-drain flux
not_answerable.why: tile-drain flow observations are missing in-domain; there is no measured drainage flux to compare against
only 160 m relief and uniform forcing; a column set is not elevation-downscaled, so any variation reflects soil not elevation

sampling_strategy.n_justification: One driver (soil texture) with ~4 dominant texture classes spanning the drainage-relevant range; 2 columns per class gives light within-class replication to separate texture signal from raster sampling noise. This is the smallest set that resolves the texture gradient without a blind grid.
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Oversample poorly-drained lowland/valley soils on the agricultural landscape where tile drainage and sub-surface drainage flux are largest and most texture-sensitive; span upland well-drained soils for contrast.
sampling_strategy.replication: 2 columns per texture class to capture within-class heterogeneity from raster sampling.

sampling_plan.reason: high-conductivity endmember; expected maximum recharge/drainage, sets the upper bound of the texture response.
dominant agricultural texture; the central reference case for drainage partitioning.
low-conductivity endmember; expected minimum drainage, tests the lower bound of texture control.
tile-drained lowlands where drainage flux is largest and most texture-sensitive; oversampled per placement logic.

validation_design.comparison: co-located where wells fall within domain — indirect corroboration of the drainage/water-table regime, not direct flux validation
none available — flagged as validation gap; could be addressed via analog tile-drainage monitoring sites elsewhere in the Corn Belt (clearly analog, not co-located)

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: baseline 1980-2018 forcing, native gridded soil per column, texture varied by stratum

requires_capabilities.why: expander must assign real texture classes per column from a soil raster
no in-domain drainage-flux observations exist to validate the target variable
to co-locate and compare simulated water-table depth
soil-moisture and drainage states must equilibrate before the analysis period
needed to attribute any drainage variation to elevation/climate rather than soil

assumptions: One representative forcing (drawn from 1980-2018) is applied uniformly across columns, isolating soil texture as the varied factor.
The agricultural landscape is dominated by a small number (~4) of texture classes that the soil raster resolves.
USGS wells, though sparse, fall within or near the domain and index the water-table regime relevant to drainage.
Native ELM does not represent engineered tile drainage explicitly; QDRAI is interpreted as the sub-surface drainage proxy.
open_questions: Is engineered tile drainage to be represented, or is natural sub-surface drainage (QDRAI) the intended target?
How many USGS wells actually fall inside the HUC 07060002 boundary?
Is a single climatological forcing acceptable, or should wet/dry years be contrasted to test texture control under different moisture regimes?
Are analog tile-drainage monitoring sites (e.g., Iowa/Illinois research farms) acceptable for process validation of drainage flux?
